description: A pure CALCULATION node — solve an OVER-determined system A·x ≈ b in the least-squares sense by Householder QR (the robust alternative to the normal equations, which square the condition number). A is m×n with m ≥ n, b is m×k. Outputs the best-fit x and the residual. Draws nothing.
instructions:
A value-only node: two matrices as JSON in (A and b), the best-fit x as JSON out. It has no geometry input or output and draws nothing on the canvas.

WHAT IT COMPUTES: the x that minimises ‖A·x − b‖ — the least-squares solution of A·x ≈ b. Use it whenever there are MORE equations than unknowns: fitting a line / polynomial / plane to many points, regression, calibrating a model against samples, or any over-determined constraint set.

INPUTS:
• valin-a — the design matrix A, m×n with m ≥ n (Grid Geometry's `val-matrix`, a point list's `val-points`, or another Matrix node). For a straight-line fit y = c₀ + c₁·t, A is the m×2 matrix [1 | t].
• valin-b — the observations b, m×k. Usually a single m×1 column; several columns solve several right-hand sides (independent fits) at once. A bare number is read as 1×1.

METHOD: Householder QR. Reflections drive A → R (upper-triangular) and b → Qᵀb without ever forming Q, then R·x = Qᵀb is back-substituted. This is preferable to the textbook normal equations x = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb (Transpose → Multiply → Inverse → Multiply): forming AᵀA squares the condition number, so QR keeps ~twice the accuracy on ill-scaled data. An UNDER-determined system (m < n — infinitely many solutions, the minimum-norm / SVD case), a row-count mismatch (A.rows ≠ b.rows), ragged input, or a rank-deficient A (a zero pivot in R) returns an EMPTY matrix — check `val-rows` > 0.

OUTPUTS:
• `val-matrix` — the solution x (n×k); plus `val-rows` / `val-cols`, and `val-value` = x[0][0] as a plain NUMBER.
• `val-residual` — the residual norm ‖A·x − b‖ (0 for an exact fit), the single-number measure of how well the model fits.

Every parameter is wireable (valin-*).
